A Custom Star-Camera Objective from Transplanted Design Forms: Double Gauss and Tessar Scaled to the IMX477

Standalone report · all figures embedded · no network required

Project: orbit-ray-tracing / orbit-oisl Date: 9 August 2026 Design tool: Ansys-independent — optiland 0.6.1 (design) + in-house sequential tracer (verification) Companion documents: objective_search_log.md (full search history), cooke_triplet_software_and_validation.md (tracer validation vs Zemax)

Abstract

Following the exhaustive failure of catalogue-element assemblies to meet a 30° field-of-view star-camera specification, we abandoned commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) elements and adopted a design-form transplant strategy: scale a published, well-corrected optical prescription to the target focal length and re-optimise. Two classical forms were transplanted — a six-element Double Gauss and a four-element Tessar — scaled to EFL 14.66 mm for a 30° diagonal field on the Sony IMX477, and optimised in optiland under a damped-least-squares merit function. Every design was then verified independently in an in-house sequential ray tracer previously validated against Ansys Zemax OpticStudio to 0.0–0.1 %. The scaled Double Gauss achieves a worst-field geometric EE80 diameter of 4.60 px against a 5 px requirement — a 7× improvement over the best catalogue-element assembly (32 px) — with 6.7× flatter field, in a 20.4 mm track using elements no larger than 8.9 mm diameter. Including diffraction the worst field reaches 6.0 px, leaving the design ~20 % short of specification on the axis, where residual spherical aberration dominates. The Tessar transplant performs markedly worse (10.2 px) for a reason that generalises: its reference prescription is a 4 mm-focal-length lens, so transplanting upward magnifies its aberrations. Independent verification caught two harness faults that produced plausible but wrong numbers, both in our own code.

1. Introduction: why catalogue elements failed

1.1 The requirement

A CubeSat star camera on the Sony IMX477 (6.287 × 4.712 mm active area, 3.9285 mm semi-diagonal, 1.55 µm pixel pitch) requires a 30° diagonal field of view, fixing the focal length at

f = 3.9285 mm / tan(15°) = 14.66 mm

with half-fields ±12.1° horizontal, ±9.13° vertical. The image-quality requirement is a spot of 3–5 pixels, interpreted as the diameter enclosing 80 % of the energy (EE80) — the quantity that maps onto a centroiding window. That is 4.65–7.75 µm. The waveband is 0.45–0.65 µm.

The motivation for building rather than buying is qualification: a custom assembly in an aluminium barrel can be thermal-vacuum tested and space-rated, which a commercial camera lens in a plastic mount cannot. A COTS Arducam 16 mm CS-mount lens covers the same field on a separate development path.

1.2 What was tried with catalogue elements, and why it failed

Six searches were run across three element pools and four architecture families (documented in full in objective_search_log.md). The results, in brief:

Architecture Best worst-field EE80
Single achromatic doublets at f/3.5 (long EFL) 28–33 px
Plössl doublet pair 52–107 px
4-element, Ø12.7 mm achromats 34.2 px
4-element, Ø25.4 mm achromats 32.1 px
5-element, Petzval-balanced (2 negatives) 58.8 px
Requirement 5 px

Three findings explain the failure, and they are structural rather than a matter of search effort:

(a) Degrees of freedom. Meeting 3–5 px at this focal length requires a near-diffraction-limited lens across ±15°: at f/4 the Airy disk alone is 3.46 px, leaving a geometric budget of ~2.8 µm. Controlling spherical aberration, coma, astigmatism, field curvature, distortion and axial and lateral colour simultaneously takes on the order of 15–20 free parameters. An assembly of N catalogue elements offers N − 1 air gaps plus focus — 4 parameters for a 4-element design — because radii, thicknesses, glasses and element bendings are frozen by the part number.

(b) Field curvature is invariant to air gaps. The Petzval sum obeys P = Σ φi/ni, and measurement across our entire catalogue showed P·f ≈ 0.63–0.73 for every stock achromat, positive or negative. Petzval therefore scales purely with element power and cannot be changed by spacing at all — a gap-only optimiser is structurally blind to it. The best 4-element assembly had a Petzval radius of 19.6 mm, giving 395 µm of corner field sag: 42× the depth of focus.

(c) The escape route is closed. Balancing Petzval requires Σφi ≈ 0, so the system power must then come entirely from element separation. But five stock achromats already carry ~25 mm of internal glass, which supplies nearly all the separation needed at f = 14.66 mm; the feasible gap window collapses to 0.3–1.0 mm. Flat field and spacing freedom are mutually exclusive with catalogue parts. Designs that achieve P ≈ 0 do so with individual element powers ~1.5× the system power, generating spherical aberration and coma that fixed element shapes cannot correct — measured at 58.8 px, roughly twice as bad as the curved-field designs.

The conclusion is not that the search was insufficient, but that the parameters catalogue assembly provides are consumed by the focal-length and field-flatness constraints before aberration balancing can begin.

1.3 The transplant strategy

Starting form dominates outcome in lens design: the merit function is violently multimodal, and where an optimiser begins determines which local minimum it reaches. Rather than optimise from scratch, we transplant a published prescription.

The scaling argument makes this attractive for our format. Aberrations scale linearly with system size at fixed f/# and field angle; diffraction does not. The IMX477 diagonal (7.86 mm) is 5.5× smaller than 35 mm format (43.3 mm), so a classical form scaled down yields 5.5× tighter geometric spots against an unchanged Airy disk:

Reference form (35 mm format) RMS there RMS scaled + diffraction at f/2.8
Cooke triplet f/4.5 15 µm 2.7 µm ~6 px
Tessar f/3.5 10 µm 1.8 µm ~4 px
Double Gauss f/2.8 7 µm 1.3 µm ~3.5 px

Our 30° field is narrower than the 46–50° these forms are quoted at, so the problem is easier than the table assumes.

2. Method

2.1 Starting prescriptions

Both forms were taken from the optiland sample catalogue, which is a published design collection (and whose Cooke triplet served as our tracer's most precise validation case against Zemax).

Form Elements Surfaces Reference EFL Reference f/# Reference field Scale factor to 14.66 mm
Double Gauss 6 (2 cemented doublets + 2 singlets) 11 100.004 mm f/5.0 ±14.0° ×0.1466 (down)
Tessar 4 (1 cemented doublet + 2 singlets) 8 3.998 mm f/4.5 ±20.5° ×3.667 (up)

The Tessar covers our field comfortably and is mechanically simpler; the Double Gauss requires its field pushed from ±14° to ±15.16°. Critically, however, the direction of the scaling differs, and §4.2 shows this dominates the outcome.

2.2 Scaling and optimisation

Radii and thicknesses scale by the focal-length ratio; field angle and f/# are scale-invariant, which is precisely what makes the transplant valid. Each scaled system was then re-optimised in optiland (pipeline/design_custom.py):

  • Variables — all finite radii and all air spaces, plus the flat cemented interfaces seeded slightly curved so they contribute usable derivatives (17 variables for the Double Gauss, 13 for the Tessar).
  • Operands — RMS spot size at three fields × three wavelengths, with the on-axis field weighted 2.5× (it carries the spherical aberration that scaling leaves behind), plus a focal-length operand at weight 50 to hold EFL = 14.66 mm.
  • Optimiser — damped least squares (optiland OptimizerGeneric).

Differentiable ray tracing was deliberately not used. At 13–17 variables a finite-difference Jacobian costs under a second, so gradient computation is not the bottleneck; the binding difficulties are starting form, constraints, and the discreteness of glass selection, none of which autodiff addresses.

2.3 Independent verification

Every design was re-traced in our in-house sequential tracer (pipeline/verify_custom.py), which was previously validated against Zemax OpticStudio to 0.0–0.1 % on RMS and geometric spot radius, 0.4 % on RMS wavefront error, and five significant figures on distortion. The transcription is direct because both tools place a surface's material after it, matching the Zemax lens-data-editor convention.

Verification re-solves the image distance to our best focus (the two tools' focus criteria differ slightly) and sets clear semi-diameters from the traced ray footprints × 1.15, which also yields the mechanical element-diameter requirement.

MTF at 165 cy/mm MTF at Nyquist (322 cy/mm)
Double Gauss 0.119 0.073

The Double Gauss retains measurable contrast at Nyquist; the Tessar does not. For a star camera this matters less than encircled energy — stars are point sources, and centroid accuracy depends on the PSF's stability and compactness rather than on extended-scene contrast — but it is a useful discriminator between the two forms.

Both transplants are 6.7–13× flatter than anything the catalogue-element search achieved, with no Petzval-balancing effort at all — the published forms simply have it designed in. The Tessar's distortion is nearly an order of magnitude lower than the Double Gauss's, which would matter for a star tracker's astrometric solution, though 1.3 % is readily calibrated.

3.7 Cross-tool verification

Quantity optiland our tracer agreement
Double Gauss EFL 14.6601 mm 14.6601 mm 0.000 %
Tessar EFL 14.6597 mm 14.6597 mm 0.000 %

Focal length agrees exactly, confirming the prescription transcription. The two tools differ slightly on best focus (0.06 mm for the Double Gauss), reflecting different focus criteria rather than a physics disagreement; verification re-solves focus independently.

4. Discussion

4.1 The Double Gauss meets the geometric requirement but not the diffraction one

The scaled Double Gauss reaches a worst-field geometric EE80 of 4.60 px, inside the 5 px specification and a 7× improvement over the best catalogue assembly. Including diffraction, however, the on-axis field reaches 6.0 px (converged Huygens calculation), leaving the design ~20 % short.

The diffraction floor is not the obstacle: a perfect f/4 lens has an EE80 diameter of 3.46 px. The gap is aberration — an on-axis Strehl ratio of 0.394, where ~0.6–0.7 would be needed. The limiting aberration is residual spherical, evidenced by the centre being the worst geometric field (4.42 px) while the edges pass comfortably (2.15–2.38 px), and by each wavelength independently showing ~3 µm on-axis RMS while the axial colour spread is only 1.0× the depth of focus.

The mechanism is understood: we are operating a reference form designed at f/5 at f/4, and spherical aberration scales as 1/(f/#)³ — a 1.95× penalty. An f/# sweep confirmed f/4 is nevertheless the combined optimum, because slowing the lens grows the Airy disk faster than it shrinks the aberration.

4.2 Transplant direction matters more than element count

The Tessar is the simpler, lighter form and covers a wider field, yet it performs 2.2× worse. The cause is the scaling direction: its reference prescription is a 4 mm focal-length lens, so transplanting it to 14.66 mm scales it up by 3.67× and magnifies its aberrations in proportion. The Double Gauss reference is a 100 mm lens, scaled down by 6.8×.

This is the single most transferable lesson of the exercise: when transplanting a design form, the reference's absolute scale matters as much as its architecture. A four-element form is not inherently worse than a six-element one; a small reference is worse than a large one. A large-format Tessar reference would very likely outperform what we obtained here, and is worth seeking.

4.3 Mechanical and qualification implications

Both designs are physically modest: 17–20 mm optical track, largest element 8.9–9.1 mm diameter, all glasses (N-SSK2, N-SK2, F5, N-SK16 for the Double Gauss) standard Schott types present in our verified catalogue. This is compatible with an aluminium barrel and a small TVAC fixture, and the small element count and diameters keep mass low. Athermalisation is untouched and will matter: an aluminium barrel has a much larger expansion coefficient than the glasses, so focus shift over the operating temperature range must be analysed before committing to a housing design.

4.4 Verification caught two faults in our own tooling

Both produced plausible but incorrect numbers, and both were in our harness rather than the designs:

  1. Wrong operand keyword. optiland's rms_spot_size takes num_rays; passing num_rings silently failed every spot operand, leaving the optimiser working on the focal-length term alone. It presented as a converged run that barely improved the spot. The merit function fell 3.5× once corrected.
  2. Degenerate trailing surface. optiland exports a residual final thickness of −2.9 × 10⁻⁸ m; an equality test against zero missed it, leaving the image plane coincident with the final surface. The Huygens integral then had zero propagation distance and returned the ray footprint instead of a PSF, reporting a diffraction EE80 of 63 px against a geometric 4.4 px. Geometric results were entirely unaffected — which is exactly what makes this class of fault easy to ship undetected. It was caught by the physical sanity check that diffraction EE cannot greatly exceed geometric EE.

Neither fault would have been visible from a single tool's output.

5. Threats to validity

  • Nominal design only. No tolerancing, thermal, coating, ghost or stray-light analysis has been performed. For space hardware, tolerancing is decisive and may consume much of the remaining margin; optiland provides Monte Carlo tolerancing and this is the next required step.
  • Sensor cover glass omitted. The IMX477 carries a cover glass and IR filter which are not in the model. Including them will shift focus and add a small amount of aberration.
  • Single optimisation run per form. The DLS optimiser reduced merit 3.5× but did not improve the on-axis field, suggesting a local minimum. Multiple starts, or explicit spherical-aberration or wavefront operands rather than pure RMS-spot targets, are untried.
  • Glass selection untouched. Both forms retain their reference glasses. Higher-index crowns would reduce spherical aberration and Petzval simultaneously and constitute unexploited design freedom.
  • The tracer's diffraction module is validated in a different regime. It was checked against Zemax on systems with 30–50 µm spots; these designs have ~4 µm spots, where the fixed analysis window initially gave nonsense (§4.4). Window-size convergence was verified explicitly for the results quoted here, but the module would benefit from a formal re-validation in the near-diffraction-limited regime.

6. Conclusions

  1. Transplanting a published design form and re-optimising is dramatically more effective than assembling catalogue elements for this specification: 4.60 px worst-field geometric EE80 versus 32 px, a 7× improvement, with 6.7× flatter field.
  2. The scaled Double Gauss meets the geometric requirement and misses the diffraction-included requirement by ~20 %, limited by on-axis residual spherical aberration (Strehl 0.394) arising from operating an f/5 form at f/4.
  3. The Tessar transplant is 2.2× worse, not because four elements are insufficient but because its reference is a 4 mm lens scaled up. Transplant direction is as important as architecture.
  4. Both designs are mechanically modest — 17–20 mm track, ≤ 9.1 mm elements, standard Schott glasses — and compatible with a space-rateable aluminium assembly.
  5. Two independent implementations remain necessary. Verification caught two harness faults invisible to either tool alone, consistent with this project's history of tool-specific errors.

Recommended next steps

  1. Re-optimise the Double Gauss with explicit spherical-aberration or wavefront operands and multiple starts, targeting on-axis Strehl > 0.6.
  2. Substitute higher-index crowns, which reduce spherical aberration and Petzval together.
  3. Source a large-format Tessar or Heliar reference and transplant downward, testing whether a four-element solution can reach specification — attractive for mass and tolerancing.
  4. Add the sensor cover glass to the model.
  5. Run Monte Carlo tolerancing before any manufacturing enquiry, and analyse athermalisation for the aluminium barrel.
